dataset.name: SPRUCE Measurements of Fine Root Production and Chemistry from Root Ingrowth Cores, Marcell Experimental Forest, Minnesota, 2022-2023
description: This dataset contains fine root production and tissue chemistry measurements from root ingrowth cores. Ingrowth cores were deployed in peat from June 28, 2022 to June 24, 2023 (2022-06-28 to 2023-06-24) inside SPRUCE Experiment plots at the Marcell Experimental Forest in northern Minnesota. The warming and elevated carbon dioxide (CO2) treatments in this dataset include +0 degrees Celsius (C) (+0 and +500 parts per million (ppm) elevated CO2), +4.5 degrees C (+0 and +500 ppm elevated CO2) and +9 degrees C (+0 and +500 ppm elevated CO2) for both hummocks and hollows, as well as +2.25 degrees C (+0 and +500 ppm) and +6.75 degrees C (+0 and +500 ppm) for hollows from minimum 10 cm depth from the peat surface. Measurements include root average diameter, root length, root biomass, and root tissue nitrogen (%N and δ15N) and carbon (%C and δ13C) concentration per plant functional type and microtopographical feature. Root length and biomass are standardized to 10 cm depth. These data were used to assess the warming and elevated CO2 response of fine roots across different peatland microtopographical features (hummocks and hollows) and plant functional types (shrub, spruce and larch).

This dataset contains one data file in comma separate (.csv) format. Additional metadata are provided: one data dictionary and a file-level metadata file in comma separate (.csv) format and a user guide in PDF (*.pdf) format.

measurementTechnique:
Study Site
Observations occurred at The Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s SPRUCE (Spruce and Peatland Responses Under Changing Environments) project (Hanson et al., 2017) at S1 bog at the U.S. Forest Service’s Marcell Experimental Forest, in Minnesota, USA (47°30.476’ N; 93°27.162’ W). SPRUCE is an ecosystem-scale study that warms the vegetation and peatland soil profile to a depth of 2 m within 12.8-m diameter open-top enclosures. The peat was heated first at – 2 m for a period of 1 year starting in summer 2014 (deep peat heating phase), then heating of the overlying air began in August 2015 starting the whole ecosystem warming phase of the experiment.

Methods
Two ingrowth cores (set A) were installed in each of the 12 experimental SPRUCE plots (with and without enclosures) on 2022-06-28. One ingrowth core was installed on raised hummock microtopography and another on depressed hollow microtopography. Hollow ingrowth cores were inserted into peat to a depth of 30 cm and adjacent hummock cores to a depth of 10 cm below the surface of the hollow. Thus, while the total length of hollow cores was always 30 cm, the total length of hummock cores varied between 25 and 45 cm depending on the height of the hummock. In addition, the cores were divided vertically into 10 cm increments, starting from the bottom of the core. This dataset includes only the topmost minimum 10 cm increments (maximum 18 cm depth from peat surface). Thus, the total increment depths varied between microtopographical features and plots. Therefore, fine root length and mass production data reported in the current dataset are standardized for this variability in depth and report all values in growth (either length or dry mass) per meter square per sampling season for a depth of 10 cm.
Root ingrowth cores were retrieved on 2023-06-24. To capture fine root growth variation between the treatments, we included the top minimum 10 cm (18 cm maximum) of the cores. Each of the samples were then separated vertically in half, whereby the first half was used for quantifying the root dry mass and fine root tissue nitrogen and carbon concentration as well as stable isotopes (δ¹⁵N and δ¹³C). Both halves were used for fine root length and diameter measurements.
Prior to sample processing, the samples were thawed in a refrigerator. The roots were separated from peat by cleaning with deionized water and separating into four dominant plant functional types (shrub, graminoid, larch and spruce). The roots were then scanned in deionized water at 1400 dpi using Epson Perfection V800 Photo Scanner (Model J221B, Epson America Inc, Long Beach, USA) and WinRHIZO Pro 2020a root scanning software (Regent Instruments Inc, Quebec, Canada). The scanning configuration included 16 root diameter classes: 0.0-0.1, 0.1-0.2, 0.2-0.3, 0.3-0.4, 0.4-0.5, 0.5-0.6, 0.6-0.7, 0.7-0.8, 0.8-0.9, 0.9-1.0, 1.0-1.25, 1.25-1.5, 1.5-1.75, 1.75-2.0, 2.0-2.25, >2.25 mm. The roots from the first halves were then dried in an oven for at least 3 days at 70 degrees C, after which they were weighed with a precision scale. All roots were considered to be fine roots, as only approximately 0.12% of the root total length fell into >2 mm diameter classes across all treatments.
After weighing, the dried roots were ground into fine powder and analyzed for fine root tissue nitrogen and carbon concentrations and root δ¹⁵N and δ¹³C using an isotope ratio mass spectrometer (Integra CN, SerCon; see quality assessment description in section 4).
Since the ingrowth core increment volumes varied between samples, and the root dry weight was measured from a vertical half of an increment, the root dry weight (biomass; g m-2) and root total length (km m-2) were standardized to 10 cm depth by taking into account total increment volume and peat bulk density.

Quality Assessment:
These data are considered at Quality Level 1. Level 1 indicates an internally consistent data product that has been subjected to quality checks and data management procedures.
Fine root tissue nitrogen (%N), carbon (%C) concentrations, and stable isotope values (δ¹⁵N and δ¹³C) were measured using an isotope ratio mass spectrometer (Delta V Advantage with Smart EA, Thermo Fisher). Quality assessment included testing whether results were affected by sample size or peak height (mass dependency), and no significant bias was found for %N, %C, or δ¹³C (p > 0.05). δ¹⁵N showed a statistically significant trend with peak size (p = 0.042), but the effect was small and not considered problematic. Calibration was conducted using both isotopic standards (USGS62 - glycine, USGS64 - caffeine, USGS25 – ammonium sulfate, and urea) and %CN standards (acetanilide, barley, alfalfa, and soils with low and high C), and the calibration curves showed excellent fit (R² > 0.997). Instrument precision, mass dependency, and sample drift was assessed with sorghum standards, with certified values for %CN and δ¹⁵N and δ¹³C . These quality assessments confirmed that the root chemistry data are reliable for further analysis.
